title: STH Q3 2026 Letter from the Editor A Moving Target
gist: In this quarterly personal/business update, ServeTheHome editor Patrick Kennedy notes that surging NAND/DRAM prices plus server CPU makers selling out capacity are reshaping what hardware is worth reviewing or buying, and predicts Q4 2026 and the following few quarters will be 'an absolute doozy' as ChatGPT-launch-era AI infrastructure bets finally ship as products.

insights.claim: Rising NAND and DRAM pricing, combined with server CPU makers being able to sell essentially all the units they can produce, is making it much harder to justify reviewing or recommending lower-end hardware platforms that would have cost less than half as much a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signals a genuine component-level supply/demand imbalance (memory pricing plus sold-out server CPU capacity) rather than a one-off anecdote; relevant for tracking margin and allocation dynamics at memory makers (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) and CPU vendors (AMD, Intel) feeding AI server demand.
insights.quote: current NAND and DRAM pricing, combined with the fact that companies can sell whatever server CPUs they can make right now, means it is getting harder to be excited about platforms that would have cost less than half as much a year ago
insights.locator: On that same note, given the cost of NAND and DRAM

insights.claim: Given current component costs, Kennedy's stance is that a new system purchase in this environment is only justified if it serves a net-new AI workload, otherwise buyers should keep using their existing non-AI systems longer because of rising system prices.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A practitioner-level capex discipline heuristic (only buy new for net-new AI use cases) that mirrors how enterprise buyers may be rationing hardware refresh budgets amid elevated memory and CPU pricing — useful signal for PC/server OEM demand forecasting.
insights.quote: if you are going to buy a new system in this environment, it should be for a net-new AI workload
insights.locator: On that same note, given the cost of NAND and DRAM

insights.claim: As a concrete illustration of price inflation, Kennedy cites a system that cost about $500 twelve months earlier now costing around $1,100, which he attributes to it not participating in the current AI hardware ecosystem's rapid pace of improvement.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A concrete real-world data point (roughly 2.2x price increase in a year for a comparable non-AI system) that quantifies the memory/component price inflation described elsewhere in the piece — a useful anchor for tracking consumer/entry-level system cost trends tied to NAND/DRAM shortages.
insights.quote: it is less exciting to review a system that was $500 only twelve months ago, is now $1100, and does not participate in it
insights.locator: Another major challenge is that the AI side feels very exciting

themes.theme: AI infrastructure buildout pace and timing

insights.claim: Kennedy predicts Q4 2026 will be 'an absolute doozy' for the server/datacenter hardware industry, arguing the market is still a few quarters away from the infrastructure bets made around the ChatGPT launch fully turning into shipped products that people will be discussing.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Implies the current AI datacenter capex cycle has a multi-quarter lag between initial investment commitments and product shipment/adoption, suggesting the buildout narrative still has meaningful runway ahead rather than being near a peak — relevant for timing AI-infrastructure-exposed equities and capex forecasts.
insights.quote: we are still a few quarters away from the bets made at the ChatGPT launch turning into shipped products and folks wanting to talk about them. This is on a path to accelerate and get even more exciting over the next few quarters

insights.claim: New local AI workstation platforms now require 400GbE networking, pushing high-speed optics into what were previously desktop/workstation-class deployments rather than only large datacenter clusters.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A leading indicator that high-bandwidth networking and optics demand is spreading beyond hyperscale datacenters into local/edge AI workstation setups, a potential incremental demand driver for networking/optics suppliers (e.g., Mellanox/NVIDIA networking, optical transceiver makers).
insights.quote: local AI now needs 400GbE, and that means more fun with optics
insights.locator: We also have several new local AI workstation platforms

insights.claim: Kennedy describes the current pace of AI hardware releases as feeling like building a PC in the 1990s or early 2000s, but happening faster, with many vendors shipping hardware rapidly and the underlying models and software improving every few weeks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Frames the current AI hardware cycle as an early-stage, rapid-iteration platform war analogous to the early PC era, implying faster obsolescence cycles and higher innovation velocity that investors should weigh against component-cost-driven hesitancy to upgrade non-AI systems.
insights.quote: It feels almost like building a PC in the 1990s or early 2000s again, but at a higher pace
insights.locator: Another major challenge is that the AI side feels very exciting

insights.claim: STH is in the midst of a new server CPU and platform launch cycle, referencing AMD EPYC Turin, NVIDIA Vera, and AMD's Helios reference rack architecture as active coverage areas, with dedicated CPU/server platform testing work (AgentSTH V7/V8) expected to accelerate over the following weeks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Flags an active, near-term wave of server CPU/platform launches (AMD and NVIDIA) that datacenter hardware investors should track for benchmark results and design-win commentary as STH's testing output ramps up.
insights.locator: AMD EPYC Turin And NVIDIA Vera

themes.theme: Monetizing datacenter/AI analysis for institutional audiences

insights.claim: ServeTheHome's analyst arm, the Axautik Group, is being built to produce paid content specifically for financial and executive communities, repackaging STH's hands-on hardware knowledge into monetizable formats distinct from STH's free public content.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Indicates rising demand from financial/institutional audiences for specialized, practitioner-grade datacenter and AI hardware analysis (e.g., a piece on data center CPUs for agentic AI), a signal that independent hardware-testing outlets see a viable paid research business model around AI infrastructure investing.
insights.quote: The Axautik Group will produce content designed more for the financial and executive communities.
insights.locator: In Q1 2025, we rolled out our new analyst arm

insights.claim: STH's Substack, launched in August 2024, is now running at over 100,000 views per month and has become an important and growing revenue source, with plans to significantly increase Axautik Group Substack content in 2026.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A concrete traction metric (100K+ monthly views) for independent, subscription-based AI/datacenter hardware analysis content, useful as a datapoint on reader/investor appetite for niche technical research outside mainstream financial media.
insights.quote: It is now running at a clip of over 100K views/ month this quarter, which is not bad.
insights.locator: There is a question of whether this will be more of a subscription model
